issues.legal_issue: A reassessment notice for a period subsequent to the taxpayer’s death is invalid.
material_facts: The challenged notice sought to reopen the assessment for 1949–50, a period subsequent to the taxpayer’s death.
issues.conclusion: The notice relating to the 1949–50 assessment year was clearly invalid.
issues.legal_principle: Section 34 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, did not validate a notice reopening an assessment for a period subsequent to the taxpayer’s death. Section 24B(1) addresses the liability of an executor, administrator, or other legal representative for tax assessed as payable by the deceased, or tax that would have been payable had the deceased not died.

predicates.reassessment_notice_challenged: A person challenges a notice seeking reassessment of a deceased taxpayer’s income.
predicates.notice_period_subsequent_to_taxpayer_dea: The period covered by the reassessment notice is subsequent to the taxpayer’s death.

issues.definition: When a challenged reassessment notice concerns a period subsequent to the taxpayer’s death, the notice is invalid.

issues.legal_issue: The validity of reassessment notices for a deceased taxpayer’s earlier assessment periods requires determining whether the tax authority identified and notified the legal representatives, including whether it made a bona fide inquiry where their identity was uncertain.
material_facts: The taxpayer died leaving a widow, daughters, and a mother, and a purported will, a compromise decree, and the management and possession of estate property raised questions about who represented the estate.
The notices were sent to the daughters but not to the mother or the trustees appointed to manage charitable property.

The tax officer did not disclose whether the daughters were identified as legal representatives under the purported will, under general law, or under the compromise decree, and did not plead that a bona fide inquiry had been made.

The respondent had obtained a share of the taxpayer’s property under the compromise decree, while the parties’ pleadings did not clarify the relevant facts or the basis for identifying the legal representatives.
issues.conclusion: The Court remanded the case to the High Court to ascertain who possessed and managed the estate, determine the status and implications of the purported will and compromise decree, and then decide whether the tax officer made a bona fide inquiry or issued notices to all the legal representatives. The Court did not finally decide the validity of the notices for these assessment periods.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 24B of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, the tax authority must proceed against the legal representatives of the deceased; where there is more than one, they represent the estate. Applying First Additional Income-tax Officer, Kozhikode v. Mrs. Suseela Sadanandan, the Court relied on Dayaram v. Shyam Sundari: where a party, after diligent and bona fide inquiry, identifies and brings the legal representatives on record, those representatives sufficiently represent the estate and the result binds the estate, including persons not impleaded. The principle is not confined to litigation and may apply to assessment of a deceased person’s income in the hands of legal representatives. The Court remanded because the facts needed to apply these principles had not been established.

predicates.reassessment_notice_challenged_in_deceas: A person challenges a reassessment notice issued in relation to a deceased taxpayer’s income.
predicates.multiple_people_may_represent_estate: The circumstances leave more than one person or group as a possible representative of the deceased taxpayer’s estate.
predicates.notice_sent_to_only_some_possible_repres: The tax authority sent reassessment notices to some, but not all, persons who may represent the estate.
predicates.tax_authority_inquiry_or_basis_unclear: The tax authority did not make clear how it identified the persons notified or whether it made a bona fide inquiry into who represented the estate.

issues.definition: When a reassessment notice concerning a deceased taxpayer is challenged, multiple people may represent the estate, only some possible representatives were notified, and the authority’s inquiry or basis is unclear, the case is remanded to determine the representatives and the adequacy of the inquiry.
